claims.text: A strong low-field magnetocaloric response in rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys is driven by an optimized distribution of nanometer-scale magnetic inhomogeneities.
The magnetic inhomogeneities arise from chemically induced lattice distortions associated with high configurational disorder.
Chemical disorder and lattice distortion create a spatial distribution of magnetic exchange interactions.
The relevant microstructure contains coexisting spin-glass-like and locally ferromagnetic regions.
The interplay between regions with distinct magnetic character produces a large, reversible magnetic entropy change at modest applied fields.
The proposed nanoscale heterogeneity promotes rapid phonon/magnon heat exchange.
The proposed magnetic heterogeneity helps maintain low magnetic hysteresis.
The proposed microstructure preserves the alloy's mechanical stability.
The initial as-cast 3d-transition-metal HEA has a heterogeneous microstructure with moderate lattice distortions.
Controlled annealing followed by rapid quenching can tune phase composition and magnetic nanodomain sizes.
The hypothesis is to be tested at fields up to approximately 2 T and temperatures around 300 K.
Annealing and quenching will increase the low-field magnetocaloric entropy change relative to the as-cast baseline.
Annealing and quenching will reduce magnetic hysteresis relative to the as-cast baseline.
Annealing and quenching will improve thermal conductivity and heat-exchange rate relative to the as-cast baseline.
Annealing and quenching will retain or improve mechanical stability relative to the as-cast baseline.
The as-cast baseline has a modest magnetocaloric effect, higher hysteresis, and slower heat exchange.
The proposed mechanism should hold primarily for rare-earth-free, 3d-transition-metal HEAs operated near room temperature.
The proposed mechanism may fail in alloys with strong magnetic anisotropy or substantial chemical ordering.
